danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: I værtshuset, foran hvilket doktorens lukkede vogn holdt, var der allerede et par fem officerer. Marja Hendríkhovna, en buttet lille blond tysker i en morgenkåbe og nathue, sad på en bred bænk i det forreste hjørne. Hendes mand, doktoren, lå og sov bag hende. Rostov og Iljín blev ved indtrædelsen i stuen modtaget med muntre råb og latter.
»Jøsses, hvor vi har det morsomt!« sagde Rostov leende.
»Og hvorfor står I der og glor?«
»Sikke nogle fine herrer! Vandet strømmer jo af dem! Gør ikke vores salon så våd.«
»Ødelæg ikke Marja Hendríkhovnas kjole!« råbte andre stemmer.

Rostov og Iljín skyndte sig at finde et hjørne, hvor de kunne skifte til tørt tøj uden at krænke Marja Hendríkhovnas blufærdighed. De ville gå ind i et bitte rum bag en skillevæg for at skifte, men fandt det fuldstændig optaget af tre officerer, der spillede kort ved lyset af et ensligt stearinlys på en tom kasse, og disse officerer ville på ingen måde afgive deres plads. Marja Hendríkhovna lånte dem beredvilligt et underskørt til brug som gardin, og bag dette skærmbræt skiftede Rostov og Iljín med hjælp fra Lavrúsjka, der havde bragt deres sager, deres våde tøj ud med tørt.

Der blev tændt ild i det faldefærdige murstenskomfur. Et bræt blev fundet, lagt over to sadler og dækket med en hesteklæde, en lille samovar blev fremskaffet samt et rejsebarskab og en halv flaske rom, og efter at have bedt Marja Hendríkhovna præsidere trængtes de alle sammen om hende. Den ene tilbød hende et rent lommetørklæde til at tørre sine yndige hænder, en anden bredte en jakke under hendes små fødder for at holde dem fra fugtigheden, en tredje hængte sin frakke over vinduet for at holde trækken ude, og endnu en anden viftede fluerne bort fra hendes mands ansigt, for at han ikke skulle vågne.
»Lad ham være,« sagde Marja Hendríkhovna med et sky og lykkeligt smil. »Han sover godt, som han gør, efter en søvnløs nat.«
»Åh nej, Marja Hendríkhovna,« svarede officeren, »man må tage sig af doktoren. Måske får han medlidenhed med mig en dag, når det gælder om at save et ben eller en arm af mig.«

Der var kun tre krus, vandet var så mudret, at man ikke kunne se, om teen var stærk eller svag, og samovaren rummede kun seks krus vand, men dette gjorde det kun des behageligere at modtage sit krus efter anciennitet fra Marja Hendríkhovnas buttede små hænder med deres korte og ikke altfor rene negle. Alle officererne syntes at være, og var virkelig, forelsket i hende den aften. Selv de, der spillede kort bag skillevæggen, forlod snart deres spil og kom hen til samovaren, idet de gav efter for den almene stemning af kur til Marja Hendríkhovna. Hun, der så sig omgivet af så strålende og høflige unge mænd, strålede af tilfredshed, hvor meget hun end forsøgte at skjule det, og så urolig hun tydeligvis blev, hver gang hendes mand rørte sig i søvne bag hende.

Der var kun én ske, sukker var der rigeligt af, men det tog for lang tid at opløse, så man besluttede, at Marja Hendríkhovna skulle røre i sukkeret for alle på skift. Rostov fik sit krus og tilsatte noget rom og bad Marja Hendríkhovna røre i det.
»Men De drikker den jo uden sukker?« sagde hun og smilede hele tiden, som om alt, hun sagde, og alt, de andre sagde, var meget morsomt og havde en dobbeltbetydning.
»Det er ikke sukkeret, jeg vil have, men kun at Deres lille hånd rører i min te.«
Marja Hendríkhovna gik med til det og begyndte at lede efter skeen, som en anden i mellemtiden havde kapret.
»Brug Deres finger, Marja Hendríkhovna, det vil være endnu dejligere,« sagde Rostov.
»For varmt!« svarede hun rødmende af fornøjelse.
Iljín hældte et par dråber rom i spanden med vand og bragte den hen til Marja Hendríkhovna og bad hende røre med sin finger.
»Det er mit krus,« sagde han. »Bare dyp Deres finger i det, og jeg drikker det hele.«

Da de havde tømt samovaren, tog Rostov et spil kort frem og foreslog, at de skulle spille »Konger« med Marja Hendríkhovna. De trak lod om, hvem der skulle danne hold med hende. På Rostovs forslag blev det aftalt, at den, der blev »Konge«, skulle have ret til at kysse Marja Hendríkhovnas hånd, og at »Fjolset« skulle gå ud og genopfylde og genopvarme samovaren til doktoren, når denne vågnede.
»Nå, men hvad hvis Marja Hendríkhovna bliver 'Konge'?« spurgte Iljín.
»Hun er allerede dronning, og hendes ord er lov!«

De var næppe begyndt at spille, før doktorens pjuskede hoved pludselig dukkede op bag Marja Hendríkhovna. Han havde været vågen i nogen tid og lyttet til, hvad der blev sagt, og fandt åbenbart intet underholdende eller morsomt i det, der foregik. Hans ansigt var trist og nedtrykt. Uden at hilse på officererne kløede han sig og bad om at få lov til at komme forbi, da de spærrede vejen. Så snart han havde forladt stuen, brød alle officererne ud i høj latter, og Marja Hendríkhovna rødmede, til tårerne stod hende i øjnene, og derved blev hun endnu mere tiltrækkende i deres øjne. Da doktoren kom tilbage fra gården, fortalte han sin kone (der havde holdt op med at smile så lykkeligt og ængsteligt så på ham i afventning af sin dom), at regnen var holdt op, og de måtte sove i deres lukkede vogn, ellers ville alt i den blive stjålet.
»Men jeg sender en oppasser... To af dem!« sagde Rostov. »Sikke en idé, doktor!«
»Jeg holder selv vagt ved den!« sagde Iljín.
»Nej, mine herrer, I har sovet, men jeg har ikke sovet i to nætter,« svarede doktoren og satte sig mut ned ved sin kone og ventede på, at spillet skulle slutte.

Da officererne så hans mørke ansigt, mens han rynkede panden over sin kone, blev de endnu muntrere, og nogle af dem kunne ikke bare sig for at le, en latter de hastigt søgte plausible undskyldninger for. Da han var gået og havde taget sin kone med sig og var faldet til ro med hende i deres lukkede vogn, lagde officererne sig i værtshuset og dækkede sig med deres våde kapper, men de sov ikke i lang tid; nu vekslede de bemærkninger og mindedes doktorens uro og hans kones fornøjelse, nu løb de ud på trappen for at berette, hvad der foregik i den lukkede vogn. Flere gange forsøgte Rostov at sove med hovedet dækket til, men en bemærkning vakte ham, og samtalen genoptoges ledsaget af urimelig, munter, barnlig latter.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: In the tavern, in front of which stood the doctor's covered cart, there were already about five officers. Mary Hendrikhovna, a plump little blonde German in a dressing jacket and nightcap, was sitting on a broad bench in the front corner. Her husband, the doctor, lay asleep behind her. Rostov and Ilyin, on entering the room, were greeted with merry shouts and laughter.
"My, how jolly we are!" said Rostov, laughing.
"And why are you standing there gaping?"
"What dandies they are! Look, the water's streaming off them! Don't get our drawing room so wet."
"Don't mess up Mary Hendrikhovna's dress!" cried other voices.

Rostov and Ilyin hurried to find a corner where they could change into dry clothes without embarrassing Mary Hendrikhovna. They were heading into a tiny alcove behind a partition, but found it completely occupied by three officers playing cards by the light of a single candle on an empty box, and these officers absolutely refused to give up their spot. Mary Hendrikhovna lent them a petticoat to use as a curtain, and behind that screen Rostov and Ilyin, with Lavrushka's help — he had brought their kits — changed out of their wet things into dry ones.

A fire was built up in the broken brick stove. A board was found, set on two saddles and covered with a horse blanket, a small samovar was produced along with a flask and half a bottle of rum, and having asked Mary Hendrikhovna to preside, they all crowded around her. One offered her a clean handkerchief to wipe her charming hands, another spread a jacket under her small feet to keep them from the damp, another draped his coat over the window to block the draft, and yet another waved flies away from her husband's face so he wouldn't wake up.
"Leave him alone," said Mary Hendrikhovna, smiling timidly and happily. "He's sleeping well as it is, after a sleepless night."
"Oh no, Mary Hendrikhovna," replied the officer, "one must look after the doctor. Perhaps he'll take pity on me someday, when it comes to cutting off a leg or an arm."

There were only three tumblers, the water was so muddy that you couldn't tell whether the tea was strong or weak, and the samovar held only six cups of water, but this made it all the more pleasant to take turns, in order of seniority, receiving one's cup from Mary Hendrikhovna's plump little hands with their short, not perfectly clean nails. All the officers appeared to be, and really were, in love with her that evening. Even those playing cards behind the partition soon abandoned their game and came over to the samovar, yielding to the general mood of courting Mary Hendrikhovna. She, seeing herself surrounded by such brilliant and polite young men, beamed with satisfaction — try as she might to hide it — and was clearly flustered each time her husband stirred in his sleep behind her.

There was only one spoon; sugar was more plentiful than anything else, but it took too long to dissolve, so it was decided that Mary Hendrikhovna should stir the sugar for everyone in turn. Rostov received his tumbler, and adding some rum to it, asked Mary Hendrikhovna to stir it.
"But you take it without sugar?" she said, smiling all the time, as if everything she said and everything the others said was very funny and had a double meaning.
"It's not the sugar I want — only that your little hand should stir my tea."
Mary Hendrikhovna agreed and began looking for the spoon, which someone had meanwhile snatched up.
"Use your finger, Mary Hendrikhovna — it will be even nicer," said Rostov.
"Too hot!" she replied, blushing with pleasure.
Ilyin put a few drops of rum into the bucket of water and brought it to Mary Hendrikhovna, asking her to stir it with her finger.
"This is my cup," said he. "Just dip your finger in and I'll drink it all up."

When they had emptied the samovar, Rostov took a pack of cards and proposed they play "Kings" with Mary Hendrikhovna. They drew lots to decide who would be on her team. At Rostov's suggestion, it was agreed that whoever became "King" should have the right to kiss Mary Hendrikhovna's hand, and that the "Fool" should go refill and reheat the samovar for the doctor when he woke up.
"Well, but what if Mary Hendrikhovna is 'King'?" asked Ilyin.
"As it is, she's Queen — and her word is law!"

They had hardly begun playing when the doctor's tousled head suddenly appeared from behind Mary Hendrikhovna. He had been awake for some time, listening to what was being said, and evidently found nothing entertaining or amusing in what was going on. His face was sad and gloomy. Without greeting the officers, he scratched himself and asked to be allowed to pass, as they were blocking the way. As soon as he left the room, all the officers burst into loud laughter and Mary Hendrikhovna blushed till her eyes filled with tears — thereby becoming still more attractive to them. Returning from the yard, the doctor told his wife (who had stopped smiling so happily and looked at him with alarm, waiting for the verdict) that the rain had stopped and they must go sleep in their covered cart, or everything in it would be stolen.
"But I'll send an orderly... Two of them!" said Rostov. "What an idea, doctor!"
"I'll stand guard on it myself!" said Ilyin.
"No, gentlemen, you've had your sleep, but I haven't slept for two nights," replied the doctor, and he sat down gloomily beside his wife, waiting for the game to end.

Seeing his gloomy face as he frowned at his wife, the officers grew still merrier, and some of them couldn't suppress laughter for which they hastily sought plausible pretexts. When he had gone, taking his wife with him, and had settled in their covered cart, the officers lay down in the tavern, covering themselves with their wet cloaks, but couldn't sleep for a long time; now they exchanged remarks, recalling the doctor's uneasiness and his wife's delight, now they ran out to the porch and reported what was happening in the covered cart. Several times Rostov, pulling his cloak over his head, tried to sleep, but some remark would rouse him and conversation would be resumed, accompanied by unreasoning, merry, childlike laughter.
